en: Now I shall explain, in due order, the meritorious sacrifice in the fire, the presentation of ritual materials, and the strengthening of the mantras.
Having worshipped the deity according to the rule, one should place [the image] in the south-eastern direction—
measuring twelve finger-breadths in width and as many finger-breadths as there are syllables in the Gāyatrī in length.
For the lower fire-drill (araṇī) is said to be six finger-breadths in height;
it should be free from all defects and produced from the heartwood of the Śamī tree.
Having meditated upon that Gāyatrī with such perfect worship,
one should likewise place the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇī), which is the Universal Soul, within her.
The mother [line] shall be at the tip of eight finger-breadths, and the field (kṣetra) shall be twelve finger-breadths;
the upilyā is said to be twelve finger-breadths, without a doubt.
With a yoke-strap of one fathom in length, made of triple-stranded cowhide and well-fastened with iron,
this is remembered as the prescribed method for the mechanical device.
It is desired here that everything be consecrated with the mantra of the God who is the Self of All;
one should indeed recite the mantra of the Universal Self and thus generate the Fire.
Having placed the produced [fire] in the vessel, one should deposit it into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The pit should be either square or circular, measuring one cubit. || 8 ||

In rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires, as enjoined by the ritual manuals, the altar should be square; however, it is said to be shaped like a vulva (bhaga) in the southeast.
In the south, there is a half-moon; in the southwest, a triangle;
in the west, a circular pit; and in the northwest, a pentagon.
Indeed, in the northeast, one should construct a seven-cornered [altar] of five types for the goddess Saumyā,
using well-baked bricks, or, if that is impossible, with unbaked ones.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as prescribed in the scriptures, in accordance with the specific mantra-homa;
for mantras dedicated to Varuṇa, however, a pitcher-shaped (kumbhākāra) pit is ordained.
Like a banner for those of Vāyu, like a thunderbolt for those of Mahendra, it is described by the best of gurus as having the form of seven tongues for those of Agni. 13.
For those of middling and superior vigor, it yields a square result;
for those of little vigor, it is triangular; and for those of feminine form, it has the shape of a vulva.
The mandala of the Raudra deities is indeed a half-moon, while that of the Saumya deities is circular;
the mandala of the Dūtīs as well as that of the Kinnaras is five-cornered. 15.
For the Vidyās and Vidyēśvaras, however, the excellent [mandala] here is lotus-shaped;
when one hundred and more oblations have been offered, it is seen to be one cubit in measure.
In the case of a thousand-fold [rite], it should be measured by one cubit on all sides;
for a ten-thousand-fold homa, it should be two cubits equal on every side.
Then, for a hundred thousand [recitations], the practitioner should prepare a pit four cubits in size;
for ten million homas, it is best if it measures eight cubits.
One who knows the ritual procedure for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should construct it level, built of baked bricks;
for all mantras, a circular pit is conducive to the fulfillment of all desires. || 19 ||
Therefore, those who know the scriptures perform the rite according to this rule;
however, when measured by a fist or a cubit, the ball [of clay] is prescribed to be two finger-breadths thick.
In the case of those equal to one *hasta* and one *māna*, it should be four *aṅgulas*;
for those of two *hastas*, it is six *aṅgulas*; and for those whose nature is double that [of two *hastas*], it is eight [aṅgulas].
For those [liṅgas] measuring eight cubits, that [height] is remembered as twelve finger-breadths;
the length should be half of the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and the width of the yoni should indeed be one part. || 22 ||
"This is the scriptural injunction regarding all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Alternatively, one may cook [the offering] in a solid, flawless earthen pit. (23)
One should construct [the altar] with the Brahma-mantras beginning with "Sadyojāta," measuring one cubit in size, at a crossroads, on a riverbank, on a mountain, or from the horn of a bull. 24.
Auspicious earth from the bank of a pond, from a field, or from the roots of *kuśa* grass;
and earth from a cremation ground, a hole, an anthill, or saline soil is not auspicious.
[This earth] should be thoroughly purified with the Aghora-mantra and adorned with a cloth.
Soaked in decoction water and mixed with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā). || 26 ||
It was sprinkled with perfumes and juices, watered with bilva-water,
and provided with gold, red ochre, vermilion, antimony, and realgar.
Having thus withdrawn [the deity], one should fashion [the image] with the Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva mantras;
one should set it ablaze, encircled by wild cow-dung, with the Aghora mantra.
One should take up the consecrated [earth] with the Īśāna mantra, but sprinkle it with the Puruṣa mantra;
then, having dug it into the ground with the Hṛdaya mantra itself, one should cause it to be established there. || 29 ||
One should carefully bake the vessel until it becomes red,
or one may leave it unbaked, provided it is very firm and beautiful.
The scraping should be performed in the center with the Aghora-weapon mantra, using the tip of a sacrificial fuel-stick (samidh) pointing either eastward or northward. 31.
There are three lines facing eastward and one line facing northward;
indeed, though they appear to run counter to the meaning of the sentence, they constitute a single unified sense.
Having performed the ritual action with the tips of the thumb and the ring finger,
and having executed the *nikuṭṭana* (stamping), one should sprinkle [the area] with water from *kuśa* grass.
Then, having spread [grass] at the crossroads, one should place the Gāyatrī upon the seat.
One should establish the forest-fire (araṇyagni) within the celestial Gāyatrī, or else [the fire] produced from a sun-crystal, or that which has arisen from the mouth of a twice-born brahmin. 35.
These two, purified by the Astra-mantra and consecrated with the Pañcabrahma-mantras,
are fit for the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) according to the procedure for secondary rites.
Having placed [the fire] with *darbha* grass while reciting the *gāyatrī*, one should immediately cover the fire;
then, one should offer the *arghya* and other honors to it in sequence by means of the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyādhipa*). 37.

When the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) has been performed in this manner, the water for the male-impelling rite (puṃsavana) should be offered with the Vāmadeva mantra; thereafter, worship is to be performed with the Rudrāṇī mantra.

Having performed [the rite] at the parting of the hair—that is, at the boundary of the womb—with the Aghora mantra, the knower of mantras should then perform the ritual of worship with the Brahmaśiras mantra. 39.
Having illuminated the birth-rites according to the prescribed rule by means of a person,
one should offer the guest-offering (arghya) with the Pāśupatāstra mantra, followed by the fragrant substances and other offerings in due order.
Then, having offered flowers with the Īśāna mantra during the ritual of naming, one should perform the touching of Śiva and worship with the Kavaca mantra. || 41 ||

Thus, the fire of Śiva becomes consecrated by the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the supreme ritual procedure, whether it be the initiation (dīkṣā), the daily rite (naityaka), or the optional rite (kāmya). 42.
Then one should perform the strewing of kuśa grass around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), as well as the placement of the seats (viṣṭara) and the enclosing sticks (paridhi). || 43 ||
With the heart-mantra arising from Śiva, which follows all mantras,
one should perform the consecration of the rice-offerings and the like, as well as the clarified butter.

One should then duly install Brahmā and the other deities with the mantras originating from the stations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in their proper sequence according to the rules; thereafter, one should perform the consecration of the sruva ladle.
Then, the *sruva* ladle should be made either of *vaikaṅkata* wood or of *khadira* wood;
it should be as thick as the joint of a thumb and as long as the number of syllables in a *gāyatrī* verse (twenty-four finger-breadths). || 46 ||
With its width spanning two thumbs and filled with astringent juice, this supreme vessel, held in the hand, brings great delight to the mind. (47)
The staff is thirty-six finger-breadths in length, six finger-breadths in girth,
with a tip seven finger-breadths long, and its circular head has a circumference of six finger-breadths.
Between the two tips of the lotus, it is beautifully adorned with well-fashioned fingers;
from the four corners situated on the lotus, it is established according to the measurement of those finger-breadths.
The hollow, the bowl, and the mouth of the *sruva* ladle are each declared to be two finger-breadths in measure;
the handle of the *sruk* ladle is sixteen [finger-breadths], including its base, and its maximum length is twenty [finger-breadths]. 50.
Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in the fire, one should touch them with blades of *kuśa* grass that have unbroken tips:
the tip [of the *sruk*] with the tip [of the grass], the middle with the middle, and the base with the base, in due order. 51.
Having performed the expiation in this manner with the previously mentioned mantra,
the knower of the ritual procedure should then perform the placing on the fire and thereafter the circumambulation with fire.

Thereafter, one should perform the purification (pavitrīkaraṇa), and then the leaping up (utplavana); then the leaping down (saṃplavana) with Darbha grass, and finally the illumination (avadyotana). 53.
Having performed the sprinkling with the *pavitra*, one should offer oblations with the *aghora* mantra;
likewise, one should offer into the eyes with the *sadyojāta*, *vāmadeva*, and *bahurūpa* mantras. 54.
Then, one should offer oblations into the fire according to one's capacity: the mouth with the [mantra] Vaktra, the head with Īśāna, and thereafter the various forms with Bahurūpa. || 55 ||
Having thus performed this entire rite originating from fire,
he should afterwards satiate the deity, having established it in the fire as before.
One should observe the colors, odors, flames, and sounds of the fire with a cultivated inner self, in order to manifest success or failure.
It was like molten gold, lapis lazuli, and rubies;
like a great rainbow, the bandhūka flower, the pomegranate blossom, emerald, and saffron.
At its rising, it resembles the sun; at midday, it has the luster of saffron-colored lotuses;
and when it rises constantly upward for those who are pure, with its crest gathered together, it is auspicious. (59)
That which is smooth, turning to the right, whose sound is muffled by the ear-canal, and which becomes fragrant during oblations of milk, clarified butter, and bilva fruit; || 60 ||
Foul-smelling, black in color, blue, or even pale-white; accompanied by the sound "ku," or harsh, lusterless, fear-inducing, and inauspicious—such is the [wind]. (61)
One should offer oblations when the fire is not yet blazing, even when it is smoky and lacking fuel;
one should offer them when it is fully kindled and licking [the offerings] for the sake of the accomplishment of the rite.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on the fire-ritual, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
Thus ends the illustrious Kriyākāṇḍa.
